summary: The reader is built to suspect everyone, chase clues that almost land, be astonished by the solution, and then be asked to judge it.

need-to-breathe.why: Nothing is built to affect the reader's breath.

hungry.why: Nothing is built to produce hunger.

full.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

thirsty.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

gassy.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

need-to-poop.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

need-to-pee.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

sleepy.why: The novel does not aim to lull.

nauseous.why: Nothing is built to sicken the reader.

urge-to-sneeze.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

urge-to-cough.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

dizzy.why: Nothing is built to produce vertigo.

fatigued.why: The reader is not made to feel exertion.

pain.why: The twelve wounds are evidence, not built to make the reader wince.

disgusted.why: Cassetti's kidnapping and murder of a child are built to make the reader share the passengers' revulsion.

itchy.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

tickled.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

over-stimulated.why: Nothing is built to overwhelm the senses.

too-hot-too-cold.why: The snowbound train is built as atmosphere that closes the world; the reader feels the cold a little.

afraid.why: A murderer among the passengers gives a faint fear; the novel is a puzzle, not a thriller.

anxious.why: The reader worries for the passengers caught in lies and for what the Yugoslav police will do.

panic.why: Nothing is built to produce panic.

sensory-pleasures.why: Nothing is built to give sensory pleasure beyond the train's comfort.

aesthetic-pleasures.why: The clockwork construction of the puzzle is built for the reader's pleasure in form.

piquancy.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

fun-excitement.why: The novel is built as a game the reader plays against the author, which is its fun.

orgasm.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

love-romantic.why: Arbuthnot and Mary Debenham's hidden attachment gives a faint romantic note.

love-family.why: The Armstrong household's devotion to Daisy is built to touch the reader once revealed.

grief.why: Linda Arden's account of Daisy, Sonia, and the colonel is built to make the reader grieve a family destroyed.

missing-someone.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

aroused-sexually.why: Nothing is built to arouse the reader.

liking-as-a-friend.why: The reader is built to like Poirot, Bouc, and, by the end, the twelve.

empathy.why: The final confession is built to make the reader feel the conspirators' grief after a book of suspecting them.

compassion.why: The Armstrong tragedy and Susanne's suicide are built to produce pity that outweighs the crime.

grateful.why: Nothing is built to make the reader grateful.

pleasure-from-helping.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

trustful-distrustful.why: Every passenger lies and every alibi is corroborated by another suspect; the reader is built to trust no one.

depressed.why: Nothing is built to lower the reader's mood.

angry.why: Cassetti's escape from justice is built to anger the reader.

envious.why: Nothing is built to produce envy.

jealous-romantic-sexual.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

jealous-friendship.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

hatred.why: Cassetti is built to be hated so that his killing can be forgiven.

contempt.why: Ratchett's attempt to buy Poirot and the Princess's hauteur draw mild scorn.

resentment.why: The reader is built to feel the outrage of a child-killer freed by money, the feeling the ending relies on.

proud.why: A reader who guesses right may feel pride, but the novel is built to prevent it.

amused.why: Mrs Hubbard's chatter and Poirot's teasing of Bouc are built for light comedy.

sense-of-belonging.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

lonely.why: Nothing is built to produce loneliness.

judgy-moral-sense.why: The two solutions are built to make the reader judge whether twelve avengers deserve the law, the novel's final question.

admiration.why: Poirot's reconstruction is built to be admired as a feat of reasoning.

embarrassed.why: Passengers caught in lies give slight secondhand embarrassment.

shame.why: Nothing is built to shame the reader.

guilt.why: The reader is made party to the merciful lie, faintly complicit.

sad.why: The Armstrong story is built to sadden once the puzzle is solved.

happy.why: Nothing is built to make the reader content beyond closure.

joyful-euphoric.why: The solution gives a surge of delight at its audacity.

effort.why: The reader must track twelve alibis, which the novel makes easy with lists.

focused-in-flow.why: The interviews and the final reveal are built to keep the reader turning pages.

distracted.why: The planted clues are built to distract the reader from the truth.

impatient.why: The reader is built to strain for the solution through twelve interviews.

curious.why: Who killed Ratchett, and how can every clue point a different way: the novel is built around the reader's curiosity.

surprised.why: That all twelve did it, and that Mrs Hubbard is Linda Arden, are built to astonish a first-time reader.

awe.why: The solution's audacity gives a flicker of awe.

skeptical-doubtful.why: The reader is built to doubt the handkerchief, the pipe cleaner, the kimono, and every alibi, just as Poirot does.

feeling-of-knowing.why: The too-neat clues are built to make the reader feel the answer is almost in reach, page after page, without landing.

confused.why: Contradictory wounds and clues are built to leave the reader baffled midway.

frustrated.why: The reader's theories collapse one after another, by design.

uncertain-certain.why: The reader is kept uncertain to the last chapter, then given two solutions and a choice.

understanding.why: Poirot's final speech is built so every clue clicks into place at once.

inspired.why: The twelve-jurors insight is built to strike the reader as brilliant.

satisfied.why: The solution closes every clue and the merciful choice closes the moral question, a satisfaction the genre promises and this book delivers.

foreboding.why: Ratchett's threatening letters and Poirot's refusal are built to make the reader expect the murder.

nostalgia.why: Nothing is built to produce nostalgia.

anticipation-suspense.why: The reader waits through the interviews for Poirot's solution, suspense the novel sustains to the end.

hope.why: The reader hopes, by the end, that the twelve will be spared.

schadenfreude.why: Cassetti's death is built to be enjoyed as deserved.

elevation.why: Poirot's merciful choice and Linda Arden's offer to take the blame lift the reader.

infatuation.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

rage.why: The reader may feel a flash of rage at Cassetti's crime.
